solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scrooge in almost complete despair

indicators.note: something almost complete is just short of its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: misery is deep unhappiness or despair

explanation.surface: Dickens's Scrooge is pictured sunk in near-total gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge is the archetypal tight-fisted hoarder, so his name stands for any such money-grubber.

clue.text: Able to move phone

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means capable of moving freely, and in Britain the noun is the everyday name for a cellphone.

clue.text: Somewhere far away protester has messed up

indicators.note: something messed up is jumbled out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, part of the anagram fodder
taken as written, part of the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A demonstrator who has blundered has been sent off somewhere remote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' reads like part of the verb 'has messed up', but it is part of the fodder, so PROTESTER plus HAS are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: The stratosphere is a layer of the atmosphere high above the earth, a place far off from us.

clue.text: A follower of The Crown?

parts.note: reads as a fan of the TV drama The Crown, but means a supporter of the monarchy

explanation.walkthrough: The Crown is a TV series about Britain's royal family, so the clue seems to ask for a viewer of it; the real sense is a supporter of the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A royalist is someone who supports monarchy or the king's cause, following the sovereign.

clue.text: Vicar joining a reactionary PM for restoration project

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is the title of a vicar

indicators.note: a reactionary looks backwards, so the letters for prime minister are turned round

parts.note: taken as written, the abbreviation for prime minister

explanation.surface: A clergyman teams up with a right-wing prime minister on a renovation scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reactionary' reads as a political label for the prime minister, but here it means looking backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A revamp is a renovation or makeover that gives something a new, improved form.

clue.text: Some samosas I ate here?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone recalls eating a few samosas and wonders where they were.
explanation.definitionFit: Samosas are a South Asian snack, so the continent is where one might eat them, the place meant by the question.

clue.text: Nick needing a break, we're told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it, so the phrase is said aloud

parts.note: a gives A; a rest is a break; with the A before it, the phrase spoken aloud gives the answer

explanation.surface: Someone needing time off, as the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is British slang for arrest, as in a police officer nicking a thief.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to nick someone is to arrest them, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Supervisor claiming time for driver's error

indicators.note: to claim is to take hold of, so the supervisor word takes the time letter into itself

parts.note: an overseer supervises workers

explanation.surface: A boss is picked out for a mistake about time, a workplace grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Oversteer is a motoring fault where the car turns more sharply than the steering wheel intends.

clue.text: State school that's going places very quickly

parts.note: to express is to state or say
to train is to school or teach

explanation.surface: A state school whose pupils are on the fast track to success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State school' looks like one thing, but splits into two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: An express train is a fast service that makes few stops between destinations.

clue.text: Crazy British fighting men

parts.note: an army is a body of fighting men

explanation.surface: A jibe that British soldiers are mad.
explanation.walkthrough: BARMY is British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is informal British slang meaning mad or foolish, a synonym of crazy.

clue.text: Papal bed somehow accommodating a corrupting influence

indicators.note: to accommodate is to house, so the rearranged letters hold the extra letter inside them
somehow suggests the letters get into place by some unspecified means, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A pope's bed somehow putting up a rogue guest, a racy little scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal rearranges PAPALBED into ABDAPPLE, and 'accommodating a' puts the clue's A inside it after the first A.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says one rotten apple spoils the barrel: one bad person who corrupts those around them.

clue.text: Self-confidence of English advance

parts.note: to go is to advance or move forward

explanation.surface: A national trait of pushing forward is put down to self-assurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ego is one's sense of self-worth, so a healthy ego is self-esteem or self-assurance.

clue.text: Unwise to be rude about king

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for rude goes around the king's letter

parts.note: impudent means cheeky or rude
R is the abbreviation for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Advice that being rude about the monarch would be foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprudent means lacking caution or good judgement, so it is a close synonym of unwise.

clue.text: Doing time? That's cool

definitions.meaning: first meaning, cryptic: keeping current with the date, as if 'doing' the time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing time' suggests a prison sentence; the question mark signals a playful reading of being abreast of the present date and time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up to date is current and fashionable, which is what cool means in slang.

clue.text: Popular and uncomplaining chap on hospital ward

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable
patient means bearing things without complaint

explanation.surface: A well-liked, stoical man lying on a hospital ward.
explanation.definitionFit: An inpatient is someone who stays in hospital overnight or longer while being treated.

clue.text: Introduce fashionable whisky-maker — only one left!

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: only one of the two L's for left stays, so the other is dropped

parts.note: a still is the apparatus used to distil whisky

explanation.surface: A trendy distillery has just one bottle remaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' is L, and 'only one left' means STILL keeps just one of its two Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: To instil an idea or habit is to introduce it gradually into someone's mind.

clue.text: A number participating in duel eventually

indicators.note: something participating in is part of the words, so the answer sits within them

parts.note: the letters run from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Someone finally joining in a duel.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a cardinal number, one more than ten.

clue.text: Thus wife becomes bearer of many young

parts.note: so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: A wife turning into a mother of a large brood.
explanation.definitionFit: A sow is a female pig, and pigs give birth to large litters of piglets.

clue.text: Reportedly goes for a cunning plan

indicators.note: something reported is passed on in speech, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: goes, as in goes to the toilet, means wees

explanation.surface: Someone opts for a clever scheme, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: A wheeze is British informal for a clever trick or scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a wheeze is a clever or crafty scheme or trick.

clue.text: Leading position a peer's had reallocated

indicators.note: reallocated means shared out again in a new way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A lord's top job has been handed to somebody else.
explanation.definitionFit: The spearhead is the front of an attack or campaign, the leading role in any effort.

clue.text: Unusual to set arm of our military against another

indicators.note: against means placed next to, so one piece sits beside the other

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, a branch of the British Army
RE is the Royal Engineers, another branch of the British Army

explanation.surface: A strange thing: setting one branch of the armed forces against another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our military' is the British Army, whose Royal Artillery and Royal Engineers are crossword staples.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare means seldom found or occurring, a close synonym of unusual.

clue.text: A place you might get lost in? Wow!

definitions.note: a verb here: to wow someone is to astonish them

parts.words: place you might get lost in
parts.note: a maze is a puzzle of paths designed to get people lost

explanation.surface: A wondering question about getting lost, then an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wow!' looks like an exclamation, but it is the verb to wow, to impress greatly.
explanation.definitionFit: To amaze someone is to astonish them, which is what wowing an audience means.

clue.text: Tanneries working purposefully

indicators.note: working suggests letters set in motion and reshaped, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Leather works going about their business with determination.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in earnest means doing it seriously and with real intent.

clue.text: Boy who picks the winners?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the machine that draws the winning Premium Bond numbers

explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE (Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment) picks winners of Premium Bonds, a British government savings lottery; the question mark marks a machine dressed up as a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie is a common boy's name and also the name of the random-number machine behind Britain's Premium Bond prize draw.
